title: Minimum Area Rectangle
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every group of 4 points directly versus treating every pair as a candidate diagonal with O(1) hash set lookups for the other 2 corners.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of points on the X-Y plane, return the minimum area of any rectangle formed by 4 of these points, where the rectangle's sides must be parallel to the x-axis and y-axis. If no such rectangle exists, return 0.

blocks.text: Among all the given points, find 4 that form an axis-aligned rectangle (sides parallel to the x and y axes) with the smallest possible area.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Smallest Rectangular Frame That Fits 4 Existing Nails
blocks.text: Picture nails hammered into a board at various points, and needing to find 4 nails that could hold the corners of a small rectangular picture frame, with the frame's edges running straight horizontally and vertically, choosing whichever 4 nails give the smallest possible frame.

blocks.caption: Any 2 points can be a rectangle's diagonal; the other 2 corners are then fully determined

blocks.text: The points (1,1), (1,3), (3,1), (3,3) form a rectangle of area 4; the extra point (2,2) does not help.
Multiple rectangles are possible; the smallest has area 2.
Before checking every group of 4 points for a rectangle, notice that an axis-aligned rectangle is completely determined by just ANY 2 of its diagonal corners.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Given any 2 points with different x-coordinates and different y-coordinates, treating them as a rectangle's diagonal corners fully determines where the OTHER two corners must be, (x1, y2) and (x2, y1).

Observation 2: Rather than checking every group of 4 points, it is enough to check every PAIR of points as a potential diagonal, and look up whether the other 2 required corners actually exist among the given points.

Observation 3: A hash set of all points supports that existence check in O(1), turning each pair check into constant work.

Observation 4: Trying every pair as a potential diagonal, and tracking the smallest valid rectangle's area, finds the true minimum.
This leads to checking every pair of points as a candidate diagonal, looking up the other two corners in a hash set, and tracking the smallest area among every valid rectangle found.
Check every group of 4 points directly, testing whether they form an axis-aligned rectangle, and track the smallest area among valid ones.

items: For every combination of 4 points, check whether they can be arranged into an axis-aligned rectangle (exactly 2 distinct x-values and 2 distinct y-values, matched correctly).
If so, compute the rectangle's area and compare it to the best found so far.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every possible group of 4 points is examined, checking whether they can be arranged as a valid rectangle's 4 corners.
This guarantees correctness, but the number of groups of 4 grows extremely quickly as the number of points increases.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n to the 4th power), checking every group of 4 points.
Space: O(1) beyond the point list.
Limitation: a rectangle is fully determined by just 2 of its corners (a diagonal pair), so checking groups of 4 does vastly more work than necessary.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking groups of 4 is wasteful: an axis-aligned rectangle's diagonal corners fully determine the other 2 corners, there is no need to select all 4 points independently.

What replaces it: check every PAIR of points as a candidate diagonal (requiring different x and different y coordinates), and look up whether the other 2 required corners exist.

How to look up corners quickly: a hash set of every given point, supporting O(1) existence checks.

The core idea: for every pair of points, compute the other 2 corners a valid rectangle would need, check the hash set for both, and track the smallest area among every valid rectangle found this way.

Store every point in a hash set. For every pair of points with different x and different y coordinates, compute the two other corners an axis-aligned rectangle would need, and check whether both exist in the hash set. If so, compute that rectangle's area and track the minimum across every valid pair.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: every pair as a candidate diagonal, hash set lookup for the other 2 corners

codes.python:
def min_area_rect(points):
    point_set = set(map(tuple, points))
    best = float('inf')
    n = len(points)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            x1, y1 = points[i]
            x2, y2 = points[j]
            if x1 == x2 or y1 == y2:
                continue                              # not a valid diagonal (same row or column)
            if (x1, y2) in point_set and (x2, y1) in point_set:   # check the other 2 corners, O(1) each
                area = abs(x2 - x1) * abs(y2 - y1)
                best = min(best, area)
    return best if best != float('inf') else 0

blocks.text: Any axis-aligned rectangle is uniquely determined by 2 of its diagonally opposite corners, so checking every pair of points as a POTENTIAL diagonal, and confirming the other 2 required corners actually exist among the given points, discovers every valid rectangle, without ever needing to select all 4 corners independently.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), checking every pair of points, with O(1) lookups per pair.
Space: O(n) for the hash set of points.

blocks.text: The key insight is that an axis-aligned rectangle needs only 2 of its corners to be fully determined, turning a search over groups of 4 points into a search over pairs, backed by fast hash set lookups for the remaining corners.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every group of 4 points", think: only 2 diagonal corners are needed to define a rectangle, check pairs and look up the rest.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n to the 4th power) time; the optimized pair-based approach runs in O(n squared) time. Space is O(1) for the brute force and O(n) for the optimized approach.

items: Pattern: reducing a 4-point rectangle search to a 2-point diagonal search, backed by hash set lookups.
Core Idea: any 2 points with different x and y coordinates could be a rectangle's diagonal; check whether the other 2 required corners exist, and track the smallest valid area.
Time: O(n to the 4th power) for the brute force, O(n squared) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: an axis-aligned rectangle is fully determined by just 2 of its diagonal corners.
Interview Difficulty: a clean example of reducing a higher-order combinatorial search using geometric structure.
One line memory trick: every pair is a candidate diagonal; look up the other 2 corners in a hash set.
